content: Oestrogen deficiency may play a role in the development of urinary incontinence in postmenopausal women. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of both local and systemic oestrogen therapies for treating urinary incontinence. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving postmenopausal women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence, or other urinary symptoms. A total of 34 trials were identified, involving approximately 19,676 women, of whom 9,599 received oestrogen therapy. Among these, 1,464 women participated in trials specifically assessing local vaginal oestrogen administration. The studies varied in terms of the type of oestrogen used, dosage, treatment duration, and follow-up periods. However, outcome data were inconsistently reported and were available for only a subset of outcomes. Systemic oestrogen therapy, particularly oral administration, was associated with a worsening of urinary incontinence compared to placebo. The combined results from six trials showed a statistically significant increase in incontinence risk (risk ratio [RR] 1.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.17 to 1.48). This finding was heavily influenced by a subgroup of women from the Hendrix trial, which had a large sample size and a one-year follow-up. In this subgroup, all participants had undergone hysterectomy and were treated with conjugated equine oestrogen. Similarly, women with an intact uterus who received combined oestrogen and progestogen therapy also experienced a statistically significant worsening of incontinence (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.18). In contrast, local oestrogen therapy, such as vaginal creams or pessaries, appeared to improve urinary incontinence. The risk ratio for improvement was 0.74 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.86), indicating a reduction in incontinence episodes. Women treated with local oestrogen experienced one to two fewer voids per 24 hours, along with reduced frequency and urgency of urination. No serious adverse events were reported with local oestrogen use, although some women experienced mild side effects such as vaginal spotting, breast tenderness, or nausea. In one large study, women who were continent at baseline and received systemic oestrogen replacement therapy (with or without progestogens) for reasons unrelated to urinary incontinence were more likely to develop new-onset urinary incontinence. Additionally, a small trial suggested that pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) was more effective than local oestrogen therapy in improving incontinence (RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.50 to 3.52). There was insufficient data to draw conclusions about the comparative effectiveness of different types of oestrogen, doses, or modes of delivery. Furthermore, the trials did not provide information on the long-term effects of oestrogen therapy or outcomes after treatment cessation. In conclusion, local oestrogen therapy may improve urinary incontinence in postmenopausal women, but systemic hormone replacement therapy, particularly with conjugated equine oestrogen, may worsen the condition. Given the potential risks of endometrial and breast cancer associated with long-term systemic oestrogen use, treatment should be limited in duration, especially for women with an intact uterus. Further research is needed to address unanswered questions regarding oestrogen therapy for urinary incontinence.
